newsitem.title: USA: Con Edison settlement needs more work.
newsitem.headline: Con Edison settlement needs more work.

text.p: Consolidated Edison Co of New York Inc's restructuring settlement with the staff of the New York Public Service Commission needs further negotiation, according to Administrative Law Judge Judith Lee.
In her recommended decision issued Friday, she said adoption of the settlement without changes, "does not sufficiently remove competitve barriers and establish a fair environment for competitors."
Lee said "the intension of this recommended decision is to offer suggestions for those areas where the parties should make additional efforts to reach an acceptable resolution."
Lee said the parties to the Con Edison settlement should be encouraged to resume negotiations for 30 additional days.
"If a revised agreement is reached, an abbreviated schedule should be established to allow an opportunity for evaluation of any new settlement," her recommendation said.

In releasing Judge Lee's recommended decision, the commission's secretary said briefs on exceptions to her views are due July 10 and briefs opposing exceptions are due July 25, when the record will be closed.

She said additional discussions "are recommended" in light of the commission staff's acknowledgement the settlement is not complete regarding matters involving the New York Power Authority and New York City. She added later that talks are continuing with the utility on the two issues.

She also cites persuasive objections, "most notably (to) those sections of the settlement involving market power concerns, specifically regarding the transportation/delivery charge component of the retail access tariff, the 80 percent in-city capacity requirement, the divestiture plan and corporate structure."

Lee said the settlement, "does not allow competition for generation and energy services" and said it "should create a fair environment for competitors at the starting point and eliminate as many barriers to entry as possible."

She said the settlement represents an extraordinary step toward resolution of complicated and contentious issues, concluding it "is certainly superior to Con Edison's October 1 (1996) filing intended to implement the commission's vision."
